source.title: Pre-train to Gain: Robust Learning Without Clean Labels
source.authors: David Szczecina; Nicholas Pellegrino; Paul W. Fieguth

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices. It has minor apparent inconsistencies, including a EuroSAT sentence referring to fine-tuning on the test set; no missing text inferred.
record.tranche_reason: The paper varies synthetic label corruption and measures clean-test accuracy, but evaluates a two-stage self-supervised pre-training pipeline rather than the original random-label fitting intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for synthetic label corruption, including clean-test accuracy, but does not report whether training error reaches zero or near zero. It tests only part of V4; it does not test fitting completely random labels, training-time cost versus true labels, unstructured inputs, explicit regularization, or the learning order of real and noisy labels.
record.test_reason: The synthetic corruption sweeps directly test V4's test-performance component: clean-test accuracy decreases monotonically as random label corruption increases. Missing training-fit measurements leave the perfect-fitting component untested; they do not invalidate the test-performance results.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that in-domain SSL improves downstream accuracy and label-error detection across datasets and architectures, with greater advantages under heavier noise. They also interpret representation and training-duration results as reduced memorization; direct noisy-label fitting rates are not reported.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a two-stage pipeline: in-domain self-supervised pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning on noisy labels. This differs from training standard networks on random labels to test memorization.
record.method_sensitivity: Pre-training method, duration, dataset, synthetic corruption rate, and initialization affect reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: In-domain SSL improves accuracy and label-error detection relative to training from scratch, including on naturally noisy datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-domain self-supervised pre-training improves robustness to noisy supervision.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 3 reports higher and more stable clean-test accuracy after SSL pre-training during 100 supervised epochs at 0.6 corruption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SSL pre-training delays deterioration in generalization during prolonged noisy-label training.

fits_no_version.finding: UMAP embeddings and silhouette scores show stronger class separation after in-domain SSL.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-domain SSL improves class structure in learned representations under noisy supervision.

record.peer_reviewed: under review at the 2027 AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI 2027)
record.problems: The paper does not report training error across the synthetic corruption sweep, so it cannot establish perfect fitting. The synthetic corruption sweep stops at η = 0.8. Main CIFAR results report means and standard deviations over five seeds, but the supplied Table 1 values omit uncertainty; the paper states significance at p < 0.05.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version rows were extracted: the reported classification and label-error detection outcomes concern the effect of SSL pre-training on noisy-label robustness, but the paper does not report training-set fitting, which V4 requires alongside test degradation. Table 1 and Table 2 contain the relevant test accuracy and label-error detection results; Figures 1–4, 6–8 and Tables 3–5 report further pre-training, initialization, and task comparisons.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels to zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Time to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed across corruption rates. Fixed training budgets and aggregate compute estimates do not measure these.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training-set fitting, degradation through fully randomized labels, and simultaneous capture of signal and memorization of noise. CIFAR corruption stops at 0.8; labels are reassigned exclusively to incorrect classes.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting, and whether removing regularization impairs clean-label generalization.

Direct comparison of learning clean patterns versus memorizing noisy labels over supervised training. SSL deliberately learns representations before label exposure; Figure 3 does not separately measure clean-label and noisy-label fitting.

missing.what: Extract the within-method clean-test accuracy sweeps bearing on V4. Baseline CIFAR-10: 83.27, 80.42, 73.00, 59.50, 27.28%; baseline CIFAR-100: 56.21, 50.03, 41.40, 27.42, 9.74%, at corruption rates 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8. SimCLR and Barlow Twins also show monotonic decreases. Although rows_left_out declares these tables excluded, its rationale incorrectly requires training-fit measurements before any V4 component can be recorded.
missing.locator: Table 1; Table 3 supplies uncertainty for the CIFAR-10 baseline and SimCLR sequences.

record.verdict_notes: No extracted rows require correction. The absent training-fit measurements warrant untested entries, not a challenge or scope limitation. Figure 3's loss axis says test loss, despite accompanying prose referring to training loss, so it cannot establish training-set memorization.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, training error, test error at chance, and keeping the original architecture and training hyperparameters unchanged.
Training time for true versus random labels and convergence as corruption increases.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.

The paper measures clean-test accuracy across synthetic corruption rates, but does not report that networks fit the training set perfectly. Its sweep ends at η = 0.8, rather than all labels corrupted.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation affect fitting random labels, or whether removing them affects generalization on true labels.
Whether networks learn patterns shared by real data before memorizing noisy or random labels.
